John — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

The apostle and evangelist John seems to have been the youngest of the twelve disciples. Jesus gave him special affection and confidence; he is therefore called the disciple Jesus loved.

John was deeply attached to his Master and, according to Henry, ministered successfully in Jerusalem and outlived the city's destruction, in agreement with Jesus' words in John 21:22.

Traditional history, as Henry recounts it, says that John later lived mainly in Ephesus, after the death of Jesus' mother. Toward the end of Domitian's reign, he was exiled to Patmos, where he wrote the book of Revelation. Under Nerva, he was released and returned to Ephesus.

Henry says it was thought that John wrote his Gospel and letters there, around AD 97, and died not long afterward. These are the commentator's historical claims and dating suggestions, not independently established facts.

The Gospel's purpose is to teach Christians the true divine nature, office and character of Jesus Christ, who came to teach and redeem humanity.

John therefore selected events displaying Christ's divine power and authority and teachings that most clearly revealed his divine nature and the atoning power of his death for the world's sins.

John only briefly described, or omitted, many events already reported in the other Gospels. In doing so, Henry says, he confirmed the truth of those accounts and made room for additional teaching and events of great importance.

Christ is the eternal and divine Word (verses 1–5)

Jesus is called the Word because, just as our speech makes our thoughts known to other people, the Son of God came to reveal his Father's mind to the world.

John plainly affirms that Christ is God.

He existed in the beginning and was with God.

Everything that has been created was made by him—not merely through him as though he were an instrument subordinate to the true Creator.

Without him nothing came into existence, from the greatest angel to the smallest worm.

This shows his complete fitness for the work of our redemption and salvation.

Both the light of reason and the life of every living creature come from Christ and continue to depend on him.

The eternal Word shines as the true Light, yet the darkness does not understand or receive him.

Let us pray continually for eyes opened to this Light, that we may walk in it and become wise for salvation through faith in Jesus Christ.

The Word enters the world as a human being (verses 6–14)

John the Baptist came as a witness to Jesus.

It shows how dark the human mind has become that even when the Light appeared, someone had to call people's attention to it.

Christ is the true Light in the fullest sense.

Every person brought into saving light receives it through his Spirit and grace.

Those who remain unenlightened by him perish in spiritual darkness.

When Jesus took on our human nature and lived among us, the Son of the Most High entered this lower world.

He was in the world but not of it.

He came to save a lost world that he himself had created.

Yet the world did not recognize its Maker.

When he returns as Judge, the world will be forced to recognize him.

Many claim to belong to Christ while refusing to receive him, because they will not part with their sins or allow him to rule them.

All God's children have been born again.

The new birth comes through God's word as the means (1 Peter 1:23) and God's Spirit as the Author.

Christ was always present in the world through his divine nature.

But in the fullness of time he came in a new way: God manifested in the flesh.

His divine glory shone through the veil of humanity.

Ordinarily, the people who know someone best discover their weaknesses.

It was the opposite with Jesus: those closest to him saw the most of his glory.

Though he outwardly took the form of a servant, his character was full of grace and truth.

His holy teaching and miracles revealed the glory of the Son of God.

He was fully pleasing to his Father and therefore fitted to plead for sinners; he also perfectly knew the truth he had come to reveal.

John bears witness to Christ's fullness (verses 15–18)

Christ entered public ministry after John, but in every deeper sense he existed before John.

Jesus was alive before appearing on earth as a man.

In him dwells all fullness.

Through faith, fallen sinners receive from him everything that makes them wise, strong, holy, useful and happy.

All the blessings we receive through Christ can be described with one word: grace.

Grace includes both God's goodwill toward us and God's good work within us.

God's law is holy, just and good, and we must use it rightly.

But it cannot provide pardon, righteousness or power to obey.

It teaches us how to live in a way that honors God's saving truth, but it cannot replace the gospel.

Every mercy coming to sinners comes through Jesus Christ.

No one can come to the Father except through him.

No one can truly know God except as the Father is revealed in his only-begotten and beloved Son.

John explains his own role (verses 19–28)

John refused to accept the title Messiah.

He came in the spirit and power of Elijah, but he was not Elijah himself.

He was also not the prophet they expected Moses to have promised: someone who, according to their mistaken hopes, would free them from Roman rule.

Instead, John described his mission in a way that urged people to listen and prepare.

He baptized with water as a profession of repentance and as an outward sign of the spiritual blessings the coming Messiah would give.

The Messiah was already among them, though they did not recognize him.

John said he was unworthy to perform even the lowest service for Jesus.

John calls Jesus the Lamb of God (verses 29–36)

When John saw Jesus, he pointed him out as the Lamb of God.

The Passover lamb—with its shed and sprinkled blood, its roasted flesh and the meal in which it was eaten—pictured the salvation of sinners through faith in Christ.

Likewise, the lambs offered morning and evening pointed toward Christ, who was sacrificed to redeem us to God by his blood.

John preached repentance.

Yet he taught his listeners to seek forgiveness of sins only through Jesus and his death.

It accords with God's glory to pardon everyone who depends upon Christ's atoning sacrifice.

Jesus takes away the sin of the world and has purchased pardon for those who repent and believe the gospel.

That should encourage us personally: if he takes away the world's sin, why not my sin?

He bore our sin for us, and so takes it from us.

God could have removed sin simply by destroying sinners, as he did in the old world.

Instead, he found a way to remove the guilt of sin while sparing the sinner, by making his Son sin for us—that is, a sin offering.

Seeing Jesus take away sin should teach us to hate it and resolve to abandon it.

We must not cling to what the Lamb of God came to remove.

John also testified to the sign at Jesus' baptism, when God bore witness to his Son.

He declared Jesus to be the Son of God and the promised Messiah.

John used every opportunity to lead people toward Christ.

Andrew and another disciple follow Jesus (verses 37–42)

What most strongly moves an awakened soul to follow Jesus is recognizing that he alone takes away sin.

Whatever fellowship takes place between Christ and our souls, he begins the conversation.

He asked the disciples, “What are you seeking?”

We should ask ourselves the same question when we begin following him.

What do we truly desire?

Are we seeking God's favor and eternal life?

Jesus invited them to come without delay.

Now is the accepted time (2 Corinthians 6:2).

It is good to be where Christ is, whatever that place may be.

We should care for the spiritual welfare of our relatives and seek to bring them to him.

Those who come to Jesus should come with a settled resolution to remain faithful and steadfast, like a firm stone.

Only his grace makes such perseverance possible.

Philip and Nathanael follow Jesus (verses 43–51)

True Christianity is following Jesus, devoting ourselves to him and walking in his footsteps.

Nathanael initially objected because of Jesus' home town.

Those who want to benefit from God's word must beware of prejudices against places and groups of people.

We should examine things for ourselves.

Often we discover good where we expected none.

Many people remain away from the path of faith because of unreasonable assumptions.

The best response to such prejudice is often simply “Come and see.”

Nathanael was an Israelite without deceit.

He was sincere rather than hypocritical, upright and godly.

Jesus knows what we really are.

Do we desire him to know us as genuine Christians?

Even true believers have weaknesses, imperfections and sins, but deliberate hypocrisy does not characterize the believer's heart.

Jesus knew what had happened when Nathanael was under the fig tree.

Henry says he was probably praying earnestly for the hope and consolation of Israel, unseen by human eyes.

This was evidence that Jesus knew the secrets of his heart.

Through Christ we enjoy fellowship with, and receive benefit from, the holy angels.

He unites and reconciles the things of heaven and earth.

[John.1.1-John.1.5]
John
The apostle and evangelist, John, seems to have been the youngest of the twelve. He was especially favoured with our Lord's regard and confidence, so as to be spoken of as the disciple whom Jesus loved. He was very sincerely attached to his Master. He exercised his ministry at Jerusalem with much success, and outlived the destruction of that city, agreeably to Christ's prediction, ch. 21:22. History relates that after the death of Christ's mother, John resided chiefly at Ephesus. Towards the close of Domitian's reign he was banished to the isle of Patmos, where he wrote his Revelation. On the accession of Nerva, he was set at liberty, and returned to Ephesus, where it is thought he wrote his Gospel and Epistles, about A. D. 97, and died soon after. The design of this Gospel appears to be to convey to the Christian world, just notions of the real nature, office, and character of that Divine Teacher, who came to instruct and to redeem mankind. For this purpose, John was directed to select for his narrative, those passages of our Saviour's life, which most clearly displayed his Divine power and authority; and those of his discourses, in which he spake most plainly of his own nature, and of the power of his death, as an atonement for the sins of the world. By omitting, or only briefly mentioning, the events recorded by the other evangelists, John gave testimony that their narratives are true, and left room for the doctrinal statements already mentioned, and for particulars omitted in the other Gospels, many of which are exceedingly important.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The Divinity of Christ. | (1-5) |
His Divine and human nature. | (6-14) |
John the Baptist's testimony to Christ. | (15-18) |
John's public testimony concerning Christ. | (19-28) |
Other testimonies of John concerning Christ. | (29-36) |
Andrew and another disciple follow Jesus. | (37-42) |
Philip and Nathanael called. | (43-51) |
Verses 1-5
The plainest reason why the Son of God is called the Word, seems to be, that as our words explain our minds to others, so was the Son of God sent in order to reveal his Father's mind to the world. What the evangelist says of Christ proves that he is God. He asserts, His existence in the beginning; His coexistence with the Father. The Word was with God. All things were made by him, and not as an instrument. Without him was not any thing made that was made, from the highest angel to the meanest worm. This shows how well qualified he was for the work of our redemption and salvation. The light of reason, as well as the life of sense, is derived from him, and depends upon him. This eternal Word, this true Light shines, but the darkness comprehends it not. Let us pray without ceasing, that our eyes may be opened to behold this Light, that we may walk in it; and thus be made wise unto salvation, by faith in Jesus Christ.
[John.1.6-John.1.14]
Verses 6-14
John the Baptist came to bear witness concerning Jesus. Nothing more fully shows the darkness of men's minds, than that when the Light had appeared, there needed a witness to call attention to it. Christ was the true Light; that great Light which deserves to be called so. By his Spirit and grace he enlightens all that are enlightened to salvation; and those that are not enlightened by him, perish in darkness. Christ was in the world when he took our nature upon him, and dwelt among us. The Son of the Highest was here in this lower world. He was in the world, but not of it. He came to save a lost world, because it was a world of his own making. Yet the world knew him not. When he comes as a Judge, the world shall know him. Many say that they are Christ's own, yet do not receive him, because they will not part with their sins, nor have him to reign over them. All the children of God are born again. This new birth is through the word of God as the means, [1Pet.1.23] 1Pe 1:23, and by the Spirit of God as the Author. By his Divine presence Christ always was in the world. But now that the fulness of time was come, he was, after another manner, God manifested in the flesh. But observe the beams of his Divine glory, which darted through this veil of flesh. Men discover their weaknesses to those most familiar with them, but it was not so with Christ; those most intimate with him saw most of his glory. Although he was in the form of a servant, as to outward circumstances, yet, in respect of graces, his form was like the Son of God His Divine glory appeared in the holiness of his doctrine, and in his miracles. He was full of grace, fully acceptable to his Father, therefore qualified to plead for us; and full of truth, fully aware of the things he was to reveal.
[John.1.15-John.1.18]
Verses 15-18
As to the order of time and entrance on his work, Christ came after John, but in every other way he was before him. The expression clearly shows that Jesus had existence before he appeared on earth as man. All fulness dwells in him, from which alone fallen sinners have, and shall receive, by faith, all that renders them wise, strong, holy, useful, and happy. Our receivings by Christ are all summed up in this one word, grace; we have received "even grace," a gift so great, so rich, so invaluable; the good will of God towards us, and the good work of God in us. The law of God is holy, just, and good; and we should make the proper use of it. But we cannot derive from it pardon, righteousness, or strength. It teaches us to adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour, but it cannot supply the place of that doctrine. As no mercy comes from God to sinners but through Jesus Christ, no man can come to the Father but by him; no man can know God, except as he is made known in the only begotten and beloved Son.
[John.1.19-John.1.28]
Verses 19-28
John disowns himself to be the Christ, who was now expected and waited for. He came in the spirit and power of Elias, but he was not the person of Elias. John was not that Prophet whom Moses said the Lord would raise up to them of their brethren, like unto him. He was not such a prophet as they expected, who would rescue them from the Romans. He gave such an account of himself, as might excite and awaken them to hearken to him. He baptized the people with water as a profession of repentance, and as an outward sign of the spiritual blessings to be conferred on them by the Messiah, who was in the midst of them, though they knew him not, and to whom he was unworthy to render the meanest service.
[John.1.29-John.1.36]
Verses 29-36
John saw Jesus coming to him, and pointed him out as the Lamb of God. The paschal lamb, in the shedding and sprinkling of its blood, the roasting and eating of its flesh, and all the other circumstances of the ordinance, represented the salvation of sinners by faith in Christ. And the lambs sacrificed every morning and evening, can only refer to Christ slain as a sacrifice to redeem us to God by his blood. John came as a preacher of repentance, yet he told his followers that they were to look for the pardon of their sins to Jesus only, and to his death. It agrees with God's glory to pardon all who depend on the atoning sacrifice of Christ. He takes away the sin of the world; purchases pardon for all that repent and believe the gospel. This encourages our faith; if Christ takes away the sin of the world, then why not my sin? He bore sin for us, and so bears it from us. God could have taken away sin, by taking away the sinner, as he took away the sin of the old world; but here is a way of doing away sin, yet sparing the sinner, by making his Son sin, that is, a sin-offering, for us. See Jesus taking away sin, and let that cause hatred of sin, and resolutions against it. Let us not hold that fast, which the Lamb of God came to take away. To confirm his testimony concerning Christ, John declares the appearance at his baptism, in which God himself bore witness to him. He saw and bare record that he is the Son of God. This is the end and object of John's testimony, that Jesus was the promised Messiah. John took every opportunity that offered to lead people to Christ.
[John.1.37-John.1.42]
Verses 37-42
The strongest and most prevailing argument with an awakened soul to follow Christ, is, that it is he only who takes away sin. Whatever communion there is between our souls and Christ, it is he who begins the discourse. He asked, What seek ye? The question Jesus put to them, we should all put to ourselves when we begin to follow Him, What do we design and desire? In following Christ, do we seek the favour of God and eternal life? He invites them to come without delay. Now is the accepted time, [2Cor.6.2] 2Co 6:2. It is good for us to be where Christ is, wherever it be. We ought to labour for the spiritual welfare of those related to us, and seek to bring them to Him. Those who come to Christ, must come with a fixed resolution to be firm and constant to him, like a stone, solid and stedfast; and it is by his grace that they are so.
[John.1.43-John.1.51]
Verses 43-51
See the nature of true Christianity, it is following Jesus; devoting ourselves to him, and treading in his steps. Observe the objection Nathanael made. All who desire to profit by the word of God, must beware of prejudices against places, or denominations of men. They should examine for themselves, and they will sometimes find good where they looked for none. Many people are kept from the ways of religion by the unreasonable prejudices they conceive. The best way to remove false notions of religion, is to make trial of it. In Nathanael there was no guile. His profession was not hypocritical. He was not a dissembler, nor dishonest; he was a sound character, a really upright, godly man. Christ knows what men are indeed. Does He know us? Let us desire to know him. Let us seek and pray to be Israelites indeed, in whom is no guile; truly Christians, approved of Christ himself. Some things weak, imperfect, and sinful, are found in all, but hypocrisy belongs not to a believer's character. Jesus witnessed what passed when Nathanael was under the fig-tree. Probably he was then in fervent prayer, seeking direction as to the Hope and Consolation of Israel, where no human eye observed him. This showed him that our Lord knew the secrets of his heart. Through Christ we commune with, and benefit by the holy angels; and things in heaven and things on earth are reconciled and united together.

Jesus changes water into wine at Cana (verses 1–11)

It is a great blessing when Christ is present at a wedding.

Anyone desiring his presence and blessing upon marriage should invite him through prayer.

He will hear.

In this life we can find ourselves lacking necessities even when we expected abundance.

At this wedding, the wine ran out.

Anyone entering ordinary worldly responsibilities should be prepared for trouble and disappointment.

When we approach Christ with a need, we should humbly explain our situation and leave him free to do what he considers best.

His reply to his mother was not disrespectful.

He addressed her with the same word in a loving way from the cross.

Nevertheless, his response stands as a warning against the misplaced worship of Mary that Henry sees in later centuries.

Our prayers may be answered when we have no idea how to proceed.

A delay in mercy is not a refusal of prayer.

Those who expect Jesus to bless them should be ready to obey his instructions.

The path of duty is the path of mercy.

We should not object to the methods he chooses.

Moses' first miracle turned water into blood (Exodus 7:20).

Christ's first miracle turned water into wine.

Henry sees here a picture of the difference between the Mosaic law and Christ's gospel.

Jesus makes the ordinary comforts of creation truly beneficial to believers.

Every work of Christ is intended for practical use.

Has he changed your water into wine by granting you knowledge and grace?

Use those blessings.

The wine was excellent.

Christ's work is good even when people fail to recognize its Author.

Henry notes that miracles produced what was best of its kind.

Jesus' action permits the proper use of wine, but it does not cancel his warning against excessive eating and drunkenness (Luke 21:34).

We may enjoy appropriate celebrations with friends, but should conduct them as though we could welcome the Redeemer to join us.

Frivolity, luxury and excess dishonor him.

Jesus cleanses the temple (verses 12–22)

The first public action John records Jesus performing after Cana was driving traders out of the temple.

The priests and leaders had allowed people motivated by greed to turn its courts into a marketplace.

People still make God's house a place of commerce when their minds are occupied with worldly business during worship or when they perform religious duties for financial profit.

After cleansing the temple, Jesus gave a sign of his authority.

He foretold that his enemies would put him to death: “Destroy this temple.”

He would allow them to destroy his body.

He also foretold that he himself would raise it again in three days.

Jesus took his life up again by his own power.

His hearers misunderstood figurative language as though it were merely literal.

The disciples understood his words after the resurrection.

Observing how Scripture's promises and prophecies are fulfilled helps us understand the divine word.

Jesus knows what is in every person (verses 23–25)

Jesus knows every human being's nature, desires, character, motives and plans.

He knows us far more thoroughly than we know one another—or even know ourselves.

He understands the hidden schemes of his enemies and the real character of those who profess friendship with him falsely.

He also knows who truly belongs to him, recognizing both the uprightness and the weaknesses of sincere believers.

We can observe what someone does.

Christ sees what is in that person's heart.

Beware of an empty profession of Christianity or a faith that is merely outward and dead.

People may deceive others and even themselves, but they cannot deceive the God who searches hearts.

Verses 1-11
It is very desirable when there is a marriage, to have Christ own and bless it. Those that would have Christ with them at their marriage, must invite him by prayer, and he will come. While in this world we sometimes find ourselves in straits, even when we think ourselves in fulness. There was want at a marriage feast. Those who are come to care for the things of the world, must look for trouble, and count upon disappointment. In our addresses to Christ, we must humbly spread our case before him, and then refer ourselves to him to do as he pleases. In Christ's reply to his mother there was no disrespect. He used the same word when speaking to her with affection from the cross; yet it is a standing testimony against the idolatry of after-ages, in giving undue honours to his mother. His hour is come when we know not what to do. Delays of mercy are not denials of prayer. Those that expect Christ's favours, must observe his orders with ready obedience. The way of duty is the way to mercy; and Christ's methods must not be objected against. The beginning of Moses' miracles was turning water into blood, [Exod.7.20] Ex 7:20; the beginning of Christ's miracles was turning water into wine; which may remind us of the difference between the law of Moses and the gospel of Christ. He showed that he improves creature-comforts to all true believers, and make them comforts indeed. And Christ's works are all for use. Has he turned thy water into wine, given thee knowledge and grace? it is to profit withal; therefore draw out now, and use it. It was the best wine. Christ's works commend themselves even to those who know not their Author. What was produced by miracles, always was the best in its kind. Though Christ hereby allows a right use of wine, he does not in the least do away his own caution, which is, that our hearts be not at any time overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness, [Luke.21.34] Lu 21:34. Though we need not scruple to feast with our friends on proper occasions, yet every social interview should be so conducted, that we might invite the Redeemer to join with us, if he were now on earth; and all levity, luxury, and excess offend him.
[John.2.12-John.2.22]
Verses 12-22
The first public work in which we find Christ engaged, was driving from the temple the traders whom the covetous priests and rulers encouraged to make a market-place of its courts. Those now make God's house a house of merchandise, whose minds are filled with cares about worldly business when attending religious exercises, or who perform Divine offices for love of gain. Christ, having thus cleansed the temple, gave a sign to those who demanded it, to prove his authority for so doing. He foretells his death by the Jews' malice, Destroy ye this temple; I will permit you to destroy it. He foretells his resurrection by his own power; In three days I will raise it up. Christ took again his own life. Men mistake by understanding that according to the letter, which the Scripture speaks by way of figure. When Jesus was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered he has said this. It helps much in understanding the Divine word, to observe the fulfilling of the Scriptures.
[John.2.23-John.2.25]
Verses 23-25
Our Lord knew all men, their nature, dispositions, affections, designs, so as we do not know any man, not even ourselves. He knows his crafty enemies, and all their secret projects; his false friends, and their true characters. He knows who are truly his, knows their uprightness, and knows their weaknesses. We know what is done by men; Christ knows what is in them, he tries the heart. Beware of a dead faith, or a formal profession: carnal, empty professors are not to be trusted, and however men impose on others or themselves, they cannot impose on the heart-searching God.

Jesus teaches Nicodemus about the new birth (verses 1–21)

Nicodemus was afraid, or ashamed, to be seen with Christ.

He therefore came to Jesus at night.

When faith is unpopular, there are many people who, like Nicodemus, hesitate to identify themselves openly with Jesus.

Yet Jesus welcomed him and taught us to encourage even weak beginnings of faith.

Nicodemus later acknowledged Christ publicly.

He was a ruler, but he did not come to discuss public affairs.

He came to talk about the condition and salvation of his own soul.

Jesus spoke immediately about the necessity and character of regeneration, the new birth, leading him to the true source of holiness.

Birth marks the beginning of life.

To be born again is to begin a genuinely new life after having lived wrongly or without proper purpose.

We need a new nature, new principles, new affections and new goals.

At our first birth we were corrupted by sin.

We must therefore become new creatures.

No stronger expression could have been chosen to describe so great a change in a person's state and character.

Something is done within us and for us that we cannot accomplish by our own efforts.

A new life begins that will endure forever.

Without it, we cannot expect to enjoy the benefits of Christ, either now or in the future.

Nicodemus misunderstood Jesus as though regenerating an immortal soul meant physically reshaping the body.

Yet he admitted his lack of understanding, demonstrating a desire to learn.

Jesus made clear that the Author of this new birth is the Holy Spirit.

Neither human intelligence nor human power can produce it.

Our corrupt nature makes the change essential.

In view of God's holiness, our own depravity and the eternal happiness promised to believers, we should not be surprised that it is so necessary.

Jesus compared the Spirit's work with water.

Henry says it is also probable Jesus was referring to baptism.

But this does not mean everyone baptized is saved, or that only baptized people can be saved.

What is indispensable is the new birth performed by the Spirit, of which baptism is a sign.

The same Greek word can refer to wind and Spirit.

God governs the wind's movement; the Spirit likewise gives his influence where, when, to whom and in whatever measure he chooses.

We may not see the origin of that work, but we can recognize its effects when a soul grieves over sin and longs for Christ.

Nicodemus still struggled to understand.

Spiritual truths seem foolish to the natural human mind.

Some people conclude that what they cannot believe cannot be proved.

Jesus' teaching about heavenly things invited Nicodemus to seek deeper understanding.

Jesus is fully able to disclose God's will, for he came down from heaven and yet is in heaven.

Here is the mystery of his two natures in one person.

He is the Son of Man, yet remains divine.

We learn these things through revelation from above, received by faith.

Jesus also taught that salvation comes through looking to him, like the Israelites bitten by poisonous serpents who survived through looking at the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:6–9).

Sin is deadly.

Whatever attraction it may seem to possess, in the end it bites like a serpent.

The remedy is set before us in the gospel.

The One we have offended has become our peace.

We receive healing by believing in Christ.

Those who despise their disease or refuse the remedy through Jesus are responsible for their own ruin.

Look to Christ crucified and live.

Unless God's grace enables us to do this, we remain wounded by Satan and under the sentence of death.

Jesus came to save us through forgiveness, delivering us from condemnation under the law.

Here is genuinely good news.

God's love is revealed in giving his Son for the world.

How astonishing that the great God should love such an undeserving world!

Our duty is to believe in Jesus Christ, whom the Father gave as Prophet, Priest and King.

We must submit to him to be taught, governed and saved.

His promise is that whoever believes in him will not perish but have everlasting life.

Through Christ God reconciles sinners to himself.

There is no other Savior.

Those who believe in Jesus are not condemned, however great their past sins.

They are not dealt with according to their guilt.

Unbelief, by contrast, rejects God's most precious gift and the only remedy for sin.

Those who reject the Son remain condemned already, under the law's charge for their sins and without the gospel's pardon.

Such unbelief springs from the heart's hostility toward God and some form of love for sin.

People performing the deeds of darkness often refuse Christ's light because it would expose their wrongdoing.

Christ is hated because sin is loved.

The renewed heart does the opposite.

It welcomes the light, wants to know God's will and obeys even when obedience conflicts with worldly advantage.

The Holy Spirit fills the heart with God's love, making that love the governing principle of life.

While a sinner is burdened by unforgiven guilt, there can be little more than fear of divine judgment.

But when the sinner sees the righteous ground of forgiveness through Christ and trusts it personally, that fear gives way to sincere love and communion with God.

Works are good when God's will is their rule, God's glory is their goal, and God's strength enables them.

Regeneration is therefore the most important concern of life.

What benefit would abundant food, fine clothes, pleasure, success or long years give us if we died without being born again and finally heard the Judge say he never knew us?

John gladly gives way to Christ (verses 22–36)

John the Baptist was content with his own assigned place and task.

Jesus had come to perform a greater work.
